daily.mode: Curated daily selection and practice rotation

lessons.title: resilient
lessons.meaning: Able to recover after difficulty or adapt when conditions change.
lessons.example: Our team stayed resilient through several setbacks and found a workable way forward.
lessons.notes: Adjective. Common patterns: resilient people, a resilient community, resilient in the face of difficulty. It does not mean never feeling upset.
lessons.conversation:
A: The first launch was rough.
B: It was, but the team has been remarkably resilient.
lessons.exercise: Describe a resilient person or group. Explain what they did after a setback.

lessons.title: resourceful
lessons.meaning: Good at finding practical ways to solve problems with the resources available.
lessons.example: With no spare parts, Maya found a resourceful way to repair the broken handle.
lessons.notes: Adjective, usually complimentary. A resourceful person uses ideas and available materials effectively; the word is not a synonym for wealthy.
lessons.conversation:
A: How did you fix it without the right tools?
B: I used what we had.
A: That was resourceful of you.
lessons.exercise: Describe a resourceful solution to a small everyday problem.

lessons.title: bring up
lessons.meaning: Introduce a subject into a conversation for discussion.
lessons.example: I did not want to bring up the budget until everyone had seen the proposal.
lessons.notes: Separable: bring up a topic / bring a topic up / bring it up. This lesson covers introducing a subject; bring up can also mean raise a child.
lessons.conversation:
A: Should we discuss the deadline now?
B: Yes, bring it up before the meeting ends.
lessons.exercise: Write a polite sentence introducing a concern you want to discuss.

lessons.title: draw on
lessons.meaning: Use knowledge, experience or another resource to help with a task.
lessons.example: She drew on her teaching experience to explain the complicated process clearly.
lessons.notes: Use draw on + resource: draw on experience, research or savings. Do not separate it: draw on it, not draw it on. Past tense: drew; past participle: drawn.
lessons.conversation:
A: How did you know what to do?
B: I drew on what I had learned in my previous role.
lessons.exercise: Name an experience you can draw on to handle a new challenge.

lessons.title: the ball is in your court
lessons.meaning: It is your turn to decide or take the next step.
lessons.example: We have sent the revised offer, so the ball is now in their court.
lessons.notes: Informal. This tennis metaphor concerns responsibility for the next move. In a delicate conversation, a direct request may sound warmer than assigning responsibility.
lessons.conversation:
A: Have they answered our proposal?
B: Not yet. The ball is in their court.
lessons.exercise: Describe a situation in which the next step depends on someone else.

lessons.title: a blessing in disguise
lessons.meaning: Something that first seems unfortunate but later turns out to be beneficial.
lessons.example: Missing that flight was a blessing in disguise: it gave me an extra day with my family.
lessons.notes: Use a blessing in disguise, not a disguised blessing. Usually retrospective; do not use it to dismiss someone’s pain before a benefit is clear.
lessons.conversation:
A: I was disappointed when the trip was canceled.
B: Did anything good come of it?
A: Yes. It was a blessing in disguise.
lessons.exercise: Describe a minor disappointment that unexpectedly led to something good.

lessons.title: Let me get back to you on that.
lessons.meaning: A natural way to promise a later answer when you need time or information.
lessons.example: Let me get back to you on that after I have checked the schedule.
lessons.notes: Get back to someone means respond later. Add a time if possible and follow through; without a deadline, it can sound like avoidance.
lessons.conversation:
A: Can you confirm the final price?
B: Let me get back to you on that by tomorrow morning.
lessons.exercise: Respond to a question you cannot answer yet. Give a specific follow-up time.

lessons.title: Inversion after Not only
lessons.meaning: When Not only begins a clause for emphasis, put the auxiliary before the subject.
lessons.example: Not only did she finish early, but she also helped the rest of the team.
lessons.notes: Pattern: Not only + auxiliary + subject + verb. Without an existing auxiliary, use do/does/did + base verb. Ordinary order remains in She not only finished early but also helped us.
lessons.conversation:
A: Was the workshop useful?
B: Very. Not only did I learn new skills, but I also met people in my field.
lessons.exercise: Rewrite: He saved us time and also improved the design. Begin with Not only.

lessons.title: Clarity begins when we name what matters.
lessons.meaning: Identifying a priority can make a confusing situation easier to understand.
lessons.example: With several tasks competing for attention, she reminded herself: clarity begins when we name what matters.
lessons.notes: Original Real Family reflection, not a quotation attributed to a historical author. Name here means identify or state explicitly, rather than give someone a name.
lessons.conversation:
A: Everything feels urgent.
B: What matters most today?
A: Finishing the application. That gives me a starting point.
lessons.exercise: Paraphrase the reflection and identify one priority for today.

lessons.title: Have you come across anything worth watching lately?
lessons.meaning: A friendly invitation to share a recent film, show or video recommendation.
lessons.example: Have you come across anything worth watching lately? I am looking for a good documentary.
lessons.notes: Come across means find by chance; worth + -ing describes something deserving your time. Lately connects naturally with the present perfect. Follow up on the person’s taste.
lessons.conversation:
A: Have you come across anything worth watching lately?
B: A documentary about city wildlife.
A: What stood out to you?
B: How animals adapt to places we overlook.
A: That sounds right up my alley. Where can I find it?
B: I will send you the link. Let me know what you think.
lessons.exercise: Recommend something briefly, then ask a follow-up question about the other person’s interests.
